title: Make a Two-Voice Zine: A Small Creative Project for Two
subtitle: A few pages, a shared prompt and two distinct points of view can turn an ordinary afternoon into a tiny handmade publication—without requiring agreement, artistic confidence or an audience.
imageAlt: Two people of different ages sit at a kitchen table, arranging hand-drawn pages and cut-paper images into a small zine.

body: A booklet with room for two

A zine can be as modest as a folded sheet of paper covered in words, drawings or cut-outs. Its small scale is part of the appeal: it gives two people a place to put their own observations without asking either person to make a speech, settle a disagreement or produce something polished. The invitation is simple. Choose one prompt, make a few pages separately, then bring them together as a booklet.

That structure leaves space for difference. One person might write a short list; the other might draw a map or make a collage. Their contributions need not match to belong in the same object. Think of the zine less as a portrait of a relationship than as a temporary shared surface: two points of view, held together by paper and a binding.
A form made for personal perspective

Zines have a broad do-it-yourself tradition: they can combine writing, drawing, collage, photographs and other forms, and they do not need a standard format. Museums and libraries now make room for them, too. Wellcome Collection's account of its zine collection describes works that bring forward voices and perspectives on health and human experience, and discusses how zines can challenge institutional categorization and representation [1]. Its account also notes that makers are consulted about catalog descriptions and can request that their zines be removed from the collection [1].

That matters even for a private project at home. A handmade page does not automatically become public property just because it exists. You and your co-maker decide what to include, who gets to read it and whether it is kept, copied or taken apart. The form can be expressive without demanding disclosure.
Choose a prompt that opens a door

Pick a prompt with enough room for different answers and no hidden test. “Something we each learned to notice” works well because it can lead to a place, a sound, a habit or a detail in an old photograph. Other possibilities: “A small thing that feels like home,” “A route we know by heart,” or “Something ordinary we see differently.”

Before you begin, agree on the boundaries. Is the zine just for the two of you? Are names, dates or identifiable family details off limits? Can either person skip a prompt or leave a page blank? These questions are not paperwork; they let both makers understand what they are making. If the prompt starts to feel loaded, change it. Curiosity is a better starting point than an assignment to reveal something intimate.
Set up the table, not a test

Gather a sheet or two of ordinary paper, a pencil or pen, scissors and glue or tape. Add whatever is already around: colored pencils, old magazines, envelopes, packaging, photographs you have permission to use. Jacksonville Public Library describes zines as DIY publications that can vary in size, length and topic; its workshop announcement says the session would focus on non-digital methods and provide materials and resources [2]. For this project, no special tools or design software are necessary.

Decide on a short working window—perhaps 30 or 45 minutes—so the activity has a natural edge. Put the materials within reach, but avoid setting out so much that choosing supplies becomes the main event. If one person likes planning and the other prefers improvising, make a loose agreement: each will create two or three pages, in any style, and no one has to explain a choice while working. Quiet is allowed. So is stopping for tea.

Fold one sheet in half, then in half again, and open it to see the panels. For a small eight-page booklet, including the covers, use a single sheet and follow a simple one-sheet zine fold: fold it into eighths, cut a short slit through the center folds, then refold and push the slit open so the pages form a booklet. If that sounds fiddly, use several separate pieces and staple, tape or tie them together instead. The binding is a choice, not an exam.

Now work independently. Each person can claim a few pages, or you can alternate page by page; choose whichever feels less constraining. Write a sentence, make a list, sketch a familiar object, paste a color or texture, or leave a page mostly empty. You might each answer the prompt directly, or respond to it in different ways. Leave room for a title if one arrives, but do not force one. You are making material to share, not competing for the most memorable page.

If one person finishes early, resist turning that into editing time. They can add a small image, take a break or simply wait. A pause can protect the slower maker’s space.

Lay the pages out before attaching them. Take turns explaining only what you want to explain; “I like this color” or “this is a place I pass every week” can be enough. Ask before interpreting a page for its maker. A collage may be meaningful, playful or just visually pleasing. The creator gets to say what it means—or to say that it does not need an explanation.

Research on co-productive zine-making workshops in Rotterdam public libraries describes opportunities for reflection and exchange, while warning that interpreting makers' pages risks overwriting their stories and voices [3]. For two people, that is a useful design principle: do not let the quicker talker become the editor of both voices. Offer each person the same chance to choose a page order, add a caption or decline a change.

If you want a shared page, make it together at the end: a map of the kitchen table, a list of words you both chose, or a page that holds two different answers. It can be a bridge between sections, not a verdict that your experiences are identical.
Bind it, title it—or leave it unfinished

Put the pages in an order that feels readable to both of you. A simple sequence might be: title, one person’s pages, the other person’s pages, then the shared page. Or shuffle them and see what new rhythm appears. Add a cover only if it helps. A title can be descriptive (“Two Ways to Notice the Garden”) or deliberately plain (“Our Zine, October”). If you cannot agree, write two titles on the cover or leave it untitled.

 The practical lesson here is permission to make the object suit its makers. Tape a loose page back in. Draw over a smudge. Let a rough edge show. If the booklet falls apart, that is a small construction problem, not evidence that the project failed.

 A home-made two-person booklet is a different scale and purpose, but it shares the useful idea that making is a way to respond to material—not just decorate it.

When the zine is assembled, decide together what happens next. You might read it once, tuck it into a drawer, make a copy for each person or take it apart and reuse the paper. Ask before photographing or sharing any page, especially if it includes someone else’s image, handwriting or private detail. Keeping the work between its makers is a complete outcome; circulation is optional.

The point is not that a craft project will make two people closer or resolve what separates them. It may simply give each person a chance to make something in the presence of the other. If one page sparks a conversation, follow it only while both people want to. If the booklet ends up funny, odd or unfinished, it has still done its job: it made a small place where two different imaginations could appear side by side.
